youtube.title: What Happens If The Strait Of Hormuz Closes
tags: what happens if strait of hormuz closed
youtube.description:
For forty years, "what happens if the Strait of Hormuz closes" was a hypothetical. A war-game scenario. A chapter in an energy textbook. On 4 March 2026 it stopped being hypothetical — and the answer turned out not to be a price.

About twenty million barrels of oil a day normally pass through a gap two miles wide: roughly a quarter of all the oil that moves by sea anywhere on earth, and close to a fifth of the world's liquefied natural gas. Eighty-four percent of it is bound for Asia.

The price shock was covered everywhere, because it was the easiest part to measure. Brent passed $100 a barrel on 8 March, the first time in four years, and peaked at $126. War-risk insurance rose four to sixfold in nine days — roughly a quarter of a million dollars per crossing for the largest tankers.

But a price is what happens to a barrel. It is not what happens to a ship. Once a vessel is inside the Persian Gulf, the only way out is the way it came in. When the strait closed, the ships already inside it simply stopped — about two thousand of them, including six cruise liners.

Those ships were not empty. In March the International Maritime Organization put the number of seafarers stranded aboard them at twenty thousand. They are, for the most part, not from the countries arguing over the strait: India, the Philippines, Indonesia, Ukraine, Romania.

And then the counts stopped agreeing with each other.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The question nobody had to answer
0:34 The narrowest place in the world economy
1:33 The part everyone covered
2:52 There is no way around
3:52 The ships stopped
4:48 The people on them
5:53 Nobody can count them
7:04 The answer

SOURCES
• International Maritime Organization, via UN News, 31 March 2026 — 20,000 seafarers stranded aboard some 2,000 vessels including six cruise liners. Damien Chevallier, Director of the Maritime Safety Division: "There is no precedent for the stranding of so many seafarers in the modern age." The International Transport Workers' Federation received more than 1,000 emails from crews requesting repatriation. https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/03/1167224
• UN Human Rights Office (OHCHR), press briefing note, July 2026 — at least nine ships with 93 crew abandoned by their owners at Iranian ports, left without reliable food, water, medicine or wages.
• gCaptain, 5 July 2026 — approximately 8,000 still stranded; an IMO figure of ~11,000 stranded across the war; ~2,900 evacuated aboard 136 ships before the evacuation plan was rescinded. https://gcaptain.com/the-race-to-rescue-8000-sailors-still-stranded-behind-hormuz/
• IMO, August 2026 — at least 6,000 seafarers aboard roughly 400 vessels remain stranded; an evacuation plan prepared but paused; "many others are unaccounted for".
• Transit volumes — ~20 million barrels/day; ~25% of seaborne oil trade; ~20% of global LNG; 84% of crude bound for Asia; China roughly one third of its oil via the strait; Europe 12–14% of its LNG from Qatar on the same route.
• Prices and insurance — Brent above $100 on 8 March 2026, first time in four years, peaking at $126; largest single-month increase on record; war-risk premiums from ~0.125% of hull value rising four to sixfold within nine days.
• Bypass capacity — Saudi East–West pipeline and the UAE's Habshan–Fujairah line; combined available spare capacity estimated at 3.5–5.5m barrels/day against ~20m normally transiting; UAE second line fast-tracked, expected operational 2027. (CNBC, March–May 2026.)

WHAT WE LEFT OUT, AND WHY
The sources genuinely disagree on how many people were stranded — 20,000 in March, 11,000 as the IMO's own figure for the whole war, 8,000 in July, 6,000 in August. The film states all four and does not choose between them, because we cannot justify choosing.

We state no running death toll. We could verify 10 deaths as of 31 March and "at least 14 civilian seafarers" in July, from different outlets on different bases; a widely-repeated figure of 17 appears only in secondary aggregation, so it is not used. Iranian-stated mariner deaths are excluded as not independently verified. No live transit count is asserted, because we could not confirm commercial tracker figures against a primary shipping-authority release.

This film states that strikes occurred on 28 February and that Iran declared the strait closed on 4 March. It does not assign responsibility for the war, does not characterise either party's motives, and recommends no action against either. Every claim it makes is about a measurable consequence.

All footage is real. No AI-generated imagery is used in this video.
